item.content:encoded:
Portuguese studio António Costa Lima Arquitectos has extended the historic Colégio de Santa Maria school in Lisbon, adding a stack of cubic concrete volumes that cascade down to a terrace and playground.

The original building was designed in the early 20th century for a Catholic religious congregation and, over the years, has undergone several renovations and extensions while serving as a residence and, subsequently, a school.

António Costa Lima Arquitectos was tasked by the current owner, the Colégio de Santa Maria, with both rationalising and improving accessibility of the existing building by adding new classrooms and recreational spaces.

This involved the demolition of an illegal annexe constructed alongside the historic building, which the studio replaced with a sculptural stack of concrete cubes that shift side to side as they rise.

"The new structure adjacent to the main building consists of a ground-up project, that is, from the foundations to the roof, a sculptural volume in reinforced concrete," said António Costa Lima Arquitectos.

"In a contemporary language, it adapts to the void created by the demolition, oscillating significantly depending on the use it offers on each floor," it added.

According to António Costa Lima Arquitectos, the shifting concrete volumes of this extension were informed by a promontory – a section of rocky, eroded land that juts out over the sea.

Alongside a new circulation and lift core that makes the historic building fully accessible, this stack contains laboratories and classrooms, and is topped by a chapel that cantilevers outwards slightly with a section of glass floor.

Read:

Habitat Collaborative threads curved school in India through tree-filled site

The chapel's cubic, carved wooden interior is visible from a new playing court below.

"The idea is to make the presence of the sacred felt in each student's daily life," explained the studio. "To this end, a window is opened in the floor, creating a visual connection between the tabernacle and the recreation area."

The new concrete volume connects directly to the historic building, where an interior refresh maintained its historic character and details.

A ramped walkway and slim concrete bridge perched on steel supports link the main building to both the new playing court at the rear and a smaller existing block of classrooms, with a paved patio in between surrounding a low concrete planter.

The exposed concrete of the extension and the walls that frame the recreational spaces has been softened with the addition of planters on the terrace on top of each of the cubic volumes. This creates a stepped series of greenery that animates the rear elevation.

Other school renovations in Lisbon featured on Dezeen include the updating of a 1950s teaching building by Site Specific Arquitectura, for which the studio created an extension punctured by large, circular cut-outs.

In France, SAM Architecture recently completed the Yvonne Kerzrého School Complex in Nanterre, arranging classrooms around cascading terraces and courtyards.

The photography is by Francisco Nogueira.

item.content:encoded:
American actor Brad Pitt has joined German filmmaker Wim Wenders on the production of a documentary exploring the works of Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

Set to premiere at the Venice Film Festival next month, From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor will be a 3D film that aims to immerse audiences in the Pritzker Prize-winning architect's buildings.

Pitt was recently brought on as executive producer of the film, which Wenders has been filming in collaboration with Zumthor for the last 14 years.

Pitt, an enthusiast of Zumthor's work, hailed the architect as a "master of light and shadow" in 2019 during a planning consultation for The David Geffen Galleries at Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), which completed last year.

Pitt "highly instrumental" to LACMA planning approval

"Brad Pitt serves as executive producer on the film, reflecting his personal support for the project and his admiration for both Peter Zumthor and Wim Wenders," said HanWay Films, which is handling worldwide sales of the documentary.

"His vocal advocacy for Zumthor's design of the LACMA building, even speaking up for the project at a decisive LA County hearing, was highly instrumental to its success."

Zumthor's expansion at LACMA is one of the buildings to feature in From Inside Out, alongside the Therme Vals spa in Switzerland, the Steilneset Memorial in Norway, the Secular Retreat house in England, the Kolumba Art Museum in Germany, the Bruder Klaus Chapel in Germany and the Wyss Building of the Beyeler Foundation in Switzerland that is expected to open later this year.

Read:

"Zumthor's LACMA building captures the strangeness of our times"

Wenders wanted to bring in the stories of those living in and visiting Zumthor's buildings, as well as capturing the materiality and design of the architecture.

"We all live and work in houses, but mostly know little if nothing about architecture," said Wenders. "From Inside Out wants to change that, not in any didactic way, but through sheer immersion and almost physical experience."

"You'll travel to remote and exclusive locations, and your guide is one of the world's greatest experts on 'the secret of places'."

Wenders directed the 2023 drama Perfect Days, which follows the life of a public toilet cleaner in Tokyo. Dezeen rounded up all 17 of the architectural Tokyo Toilets that featured in the Oscar-nominated film.

Last year, a docu-drama by filmmaker Beatrice Minger on the E-1027 house sought to highlight the boundary-pushing work of modernist architect Eileen Gray.

item.content:encoded:
With a renewed focus on contemporary art, Groninger Museum artistic director Roos Gortzak is seeking closer connection between the extraordinary postmodern building, she says in this interview.

"I think you always have to start as a curator with where you're at – so I would never have made the same artistic course somewhere else as I'm doing here," Gortzak tells Dezeen.

"Some museums are so neutral that maybe you could kind of be anywhere, but with our building, there's no way to get around the building."

Opened in 1994, the Groninger Museum building is totally unique.

In a classic postmodern twist, it was conceived as three bridge-connected pavilions, each designed by a separate architect given plenty of creative freedom.

Italian designer and architect Alessandro Mendini, coordinating the project, erected a windowless yellow tower at the centre flanked by two volumes, one pink and one green.

On one side of this central structure lies a shiny metal cylinder designed by French designer Philippe Starck, sitting atop a fort-like brick plinth by Memphis Group member Michele De Lucchi.

And on the other, a madcap deconstructivist building by Austrian firm Coop Himmelb(l)au, bursting with colour and bursting out of itself.

"Very resonant with our times"

Despite its eye-popping architecture, and despite occupying a prominent spot in Groningen on an island in the canal linking the main station to the city centre, the museum has had nothing like the impact of Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao, which opened three years later.

"It totally deserves to be more famous," Gortzak enthused.

"I'm never that interested in fame in and of itself," she added. "But I think there are so many important values that should be shared within these times, where people are more afraid of life in general, and of neighbours who might vote for other parties, and how do you find how do you find each other again, how do you connect?"

"I think all of these things are within this building, which I find exciting, and that's why I think it deserves indeed to be more well known, and be an example for many other museums."

It's a "very difficult moment" for museums generally, she added, with many facing declining visitor numbers and intensifying funding pressures.

"There's many ways to spend your free time, and also many ways to inform yourself, and so I think it's not self-evident to go to a museum," said Gortzak.

"I don't think that's a bad thing, but it's something you have to take into account developing new stories for museums," she added. "It's very important to think about how you can keep a museum relevant in these times."

Gortzak's career as an art curator and critic spans more than 25 years and multiple nations. She joined the Groninger in February 2025, having previously spent a decade as director of the Vleeshal Center for Contemporary Art in Middelburg, at the other end of the country.

Now fully settled in, she is setting out her long-term vision for the institution, with renewed programming beginning in September.

"It's going back to the future, examining the DNA of the iconic postmodern building, and proposes radically remembering the path that was laid in the 1990s when contemporary art was at the centre of the programming, and recommitting to this approach," Gortzak explained.

"Your difference is welcome here"

In deciding the future direction of the museum's curation she has taken its architecture as a starting point, inferring three core values from the building: "experimental"; "interdisciplinary"; "collective".

"The core values of the building are very resonant with our times," she remarked.

Part of her ambition is to redress an imbalance in the types of creative voices that have historically been platformed at the Groninger – not least through the fact it was designed by four men.

As a result, the new programme will involve acquiring contemporary art that is mainly woman- or non-binary-led, which she says have previously been "sorely missing from the conversation".

She considers the push for greater diversity to be wholly in-keeping with the museum's collaborative approach to architecture.

"It's already ingrained within the building to not be afraid of different voices," she said. "As opposed to one voice who tells you what art capital 'A' is, or architecture capital 'A' is, it's already really going against that."

"A museum is a place for everyone to go to, where many voices can be heard, and the museum is kind of screaming 'your difference is welcome here' through the building."

For Gortzak, the connections between the museum's architecture and contemporary art don't stop there, however.

She also notes, for instance, that unlike many art museums where a staircase leads up from the entrance hall into the exhibitions, visitors at the Groninger must head downstairs.

"So it's going away from this idea where you have to go up and be elevated through art," she said. "It's kind of saying art's everywhere, and you go down to find it."

Read:

NL Architects unveils Forum Groningen as a "cultural department store"

Meanwhile, the building is easy to get lost in by design – with Gortzak drawing a parallel with the challenging nature of contemporary art.

"You don't always have to like or understand something," she said. "It's so important to be in spaces where you are confronted with something else, and maybe you feel uncomfortable, but that's good."

Gortzak also points to an element of the building's backstory. The Coop Himmelb(l)au pavilion was initially supposed to be designed by American artist Frank Stella.

But after more than a year of work, his plan to build a structure entirely out of Teflon was deemed too expensive, and abandoned.

"This experiment, I think, that's very radical and it's very exciting," said Gortzak. "And things should also be able to fail. Not everything has to be successful, and I think art needs to create that space for that, and contemporary art also."

"We're looking for the voices that were unheard"

Some aspects of the building's design have shown themselves to be ahead of the curve, Gortzak suggests.

For example, Mendini prescribed a palette of 22 different colours that could be selected for exhibition walls – a clear divergence from the traditional white, which many other galleries are also now moving away from.

"But with us, it's not just like adding a decorative layer," said Gortzak. "It's actually part of the conceptual core of the building."

Other elements can be challenging – such as the presence of curved walls in two of the exhibition spaces, though Gortzak insists she enjoys the challenge.

The museum's new programme will commence next month with four interconnected exhibitions opening simultaneously.

One of them is entitled The Architect and the Housewife: Cleaning the House, Building the Future.

It will explore power dynamics in daily and domestic life, as well as some of the similarities between the behind-the-scenes problem-solving of architecture and of housework.

Exhibits will include a model of Zaha Hadid's Music Video Pavilion – an installation for a 1990 festival in Groningen – and a collection of 98 vases made by Mendini and decorated by a series of designers, including himself working under a female pseudonym.

For a year the museum's programme will revolve around the two characters of the architect and the housewife, as a springboard for discussions about who is allowed to think big, and how creative endeavours can be balanced with the demands of the everyday.

"In our times where we're looking for the voices that were unheard, the histories that were unseen, the unspoken role of invisible labour, I think it's super exciting to be with this building that has all of that in it," said Gortzak.

item.content:encoded:
AIM Architecture has designed Zara Huaihai Road, a flagship store for the Spanish fashion brand in Shanghai, with an amphitheatre-like brick podium that connects the building with the street.

Located on Huaihai Road, a well-known commercial district in central Shanghai, the new flagship store took over an existing five-storey concrete building, which AIM Architecture aimed to transform into a space for discovery.

"Rather than imposing a new identity, the design embraces the building's existing concrete structure, proportions, and spatial logic, allowing the architecture itself to shape the experience," said AIM Architecture.

"The project reflects Zara's evolution towards more open, flexible, and immersive environments, where the journey is as meaningful as the destination," it added.

The studio opened up the facade on the ground level by creating a stepped brick podium that extends onto the street.

Passersby are encouraged to sit down and rest at the amphitheatre-like structure, which is planted with green shrubs and sheltered by the building.

A similar, smaller brick podium was created inside the store, near the entrance. This podium, which functions partially as stairs and seating and partially as product display, connects the visual language of the store interior with its exterior.

At the Zara Huaihai Road store, the fashion brand's collections are spread over the building's five floors, where they are presented in different interiors to suit the different styles.

Zara's TRF collection sits within a space that resembles a contemporary warehouse, while the main women's fashion collection is shown in an art gallery-like environment.

The menswear floor was divided into two spaces: an atelier celebrating craftsmanship and a contemporary Shanghai loft that was designed to have a more domestic feel.

AIM Architecture covered the fitting rooms in mirrors to create a more immersive feeling.

Read:

AIM Architecture transforms oil silos in China into community park

Throughout the store, exposed structural columns, polished concrete floors and a concrete cassette ceiling were used to create a raw, industrial atmosphere, while timber and linen add warmth and tactility.

Lightweight and adaptable furniture and display systems were introduced to allow for flexible seasonal display changes.

AIM Architecture kept the building's existing staircase, but redesigned it to have a more sculptural shape.

It paired the staircase's concrete steps with a black textured-steel railing, which was wrapped in serrated concrete at the lower end. A thin lighting tube hangs at the centre of the stairwell, illuminating the otherwise dark space.

"Zara Huaihai Road reflects a broader vision for the future of physical retail," said AIM Architecture.

"By embracing the existing architecture rather than replacing it, the project transforms a commercial building into a contemporary public interior rooted in the life of Shanghai, creating destinations where commerce, culture, and community converge."

Founded by Belgian and Dutch architects Wendy Saunders and Vincent de Graaf in 2005, AIM Architecture now has offices in Shanghai, Antwerp, Hong Kong and Chicago. It was awarded Interior Designer of the Year at Dezeen Awards China in 2023.

Previously in China, it has completed a resort in Chengdu featuring sweeping, tentacle-like canopies, as well as a community park repurposed from oil silos in Changzhou.

The photography is by Seth Powers.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Xiang Architects has unveiled a multi-stair observation tower within the Chenhu Wetland bird sanctuary near Wuhan City, China.

Named the Chenhu Migratory Bird Observation Tower, the viewpoint rises 19.8 metres above the surrounding marshland that becomes home to over 100,000 migratory birds every winter.

Shanghai-based Xiang Architects designed the watchtower to be almost entirely formed of stairs, arranged in a double helix to create a continuous route up and down the viewpoint.

Each staircase terminates at a short balcony-like space with a glazed section, creating 24 staggered viewing platforms.

"The experience is organised into three perceptual stages: ascending, turning, and overlooking," said Xiang Architects.

"The stairs establish a steady physical rhythm, while the platforms provide moments of pause and reflection."

Read:

Ten viewpoints where dramatic architecture rivals the landscape

"By the time visitors reach the summit, the final panoramic view feels like the climax of a journey rather than an isolated visual event," it continued.

"The landscape is not just a destination; it is a continuous narrative shaped by movement."

The staircases also act as the tower's primary structure, in what the studio said is a move "away from the conventional central core".

Built from 24 standardised, prefabricated elements, the staircases wrap around a central, three-metre-wide void. The structure is supported by counter-rotated steel braces.

Chenhu Migratory Bird Observation Tower was entirely clad in steel to give it a distinctive appearance that stands out from the surrounding natural landscape.

"It captures the shifting atmosphere – dissolving into the wetland mist on overcast days, reflecting the clear blue sky, and glowing with the warm amber of the sunset," said the studio.

"Rather than attempting to hide or mimic nature, the tower maintains a clear architectural presence, engaging with its surroundings through a constant interplay of light and materiality."

Chenhu Migratory Bird Observation Tower is the latest architecturally interesting viewpoint to be featured on Dezeen. We recently rounded up 10 viewpoints where dramatic architecture rivals the landscape, including the Titlis Tower by Herzog & de Meuron.

item.content:encoded:
The American Institute of Architecture has announced the longest ever slump in architecture revenues in the US measured by the ABI index, citing "macroeconomic uncertainty" associated with rising oil prices.

Today, the July report of the AIA/Deltek Architecture Billings Index (ABI), an index tracking non-residential construction in the American architecture industry since the 1990s, cited a decrease from June to July in its metrics.

The decrease is part of a downward slope that has lasted three and a half years, according to the American Institute of Architects (AIA) – the longest since the ABI began.

"This ongoing slump in business conditions has now stretched to nearly three and a half years, the longest in the ABI's history," said the AIA.

Contract value falling

The report was tempered by a note of client interest and an increase in inquiries across the industry, but also noted a decrease in the value of signed contracts.

"Clients continue to show interest, as inquiries for new projects rose again in July, though more slowly than in June. At the same time, the value of newly signed design contracts fell further after coming close to growth the previous month."

Out of the four regions the index tracks, the American Northeast had the biggest slump, with a score of 44.8, with 50 meaning no growth or decrease. The other three regions showed slight upticks from lows earlier in the year.

The overall index put July at 46.6.

Read:

First images of Gensler-designed 60-building data centre development in Utah revealed

The slump covered all areas of specialisation tracked by the index.

"Billings fell across every specialization," said the AIA.

"Firms with multifamily residential and institutional specializations posted slight growth earlier this year but have since seen conditions soften. Firms with a commercial and industrial specialization have not reported a rise in billings since July four years ago."

"High oil prices are putting upward pressure on inflation"

According to AIA chief economist Richard Branch, general economic conditions are driving the slump.

"Macroeconomic uncertainty continues to weigh on the built environment," said Branch.

"High oil prices are putting upward pressure on inflation and may lead to even higher rates in the back half of the year. This will put additional pressure on developers and may lead to a further weakening in billings."

This fall in revenues is happening at the same time as rising construction costs. According to the Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) research on Bureau of Labor Statistics data, construction prices have risen as much as 7.4 per cent year over year since July 2025.

Read:

How architecture fees got so low

While the stretch is technically the longest the index has been in the negative, a spokesperson from the AIA noted that the billings today are nowhere near the lows of 2020 during Covid, when they reached as low as 29.6.

The longest stretch before was around 30 months following the 2008 recession.

Last year, Dezeen took a look at problems facing the architecture industry, including a general lowness of fees.

item.content:encoded:
Texas studio Schaum Architects has joined a team of restorers to work on the two massive Artillery Sheds at the Chinati Foundation, the museum artist Donald Judd set up in Marfa to act as permanent storehouses and exhibition spaces for his work.

Schaum Architects will serve as design architect on the project to restore the structures. Originally 1930s military sheds, they were repurposed by Judd in the 1980s, when the artist added the Quonset-hut style roofs and replaced the garage doors with quartered windows.

The Artillery Sheds holds Judd's milled-aluminium works. The goal of the renovation is to keep the buildings as true to Judd's vision as possible, while updating them for contemporary mechanical systems.

Schaum Architects founder Troy Schaum said that his studio will take the approach of "editing around the edges".

“We have to think about this work in an integrated way because there is no real envelope – the interior and exterior of the buildings are linked," he told Dezeen. "It's not as if we are repairing the buildings, then restoring the landscape. We have to think about these elements together."

The studio will work alongside members of the Chinati Foundation such as executive director Caitlin Murray, director of preservation and planning Stephen Martin and head of conservation Bogna Skwara, as well as a team of specialists.

In terms of interventions, Schaum noted the implementation of kicker braces around the edges of the metal roof that will create "properly sized gutters for the first time" and better secure the roof against the wind.

Water runoff from the new gutter system will feed the restored landscape system planned for the site by Houston-based Dept LLC with local landscape designer Jim Martinez.

The landscape aspect will include restoration of parts of the site still degraded from its former military use as well as the implementation of an ADA-compliant walking path.

Read:

Six "not so unusual" furniture pieces by Donald Judd

According to Schaum, another challenging aspect of the renovation will be air conditioning.

Currently, the building runs without any mechanical systems, and the team is seeking to maintain the quiet and low-carbon operation of the building.

They will use the already existing concrete expansion joints to install low-energy, solar-powered filtration systems to circulate air – and re-treat and replace the glass on the facade.

"The design answer is a system visitors will never see or hear," said the architecture studio.

"Using the existing opening and breaks caused by concrete expansion joints, minimal filtered fresh air will circulate in the space. The treatment of the glass will create positive pressure to exclude dust and bring down temperatures to acceptable levels."

"The goal is to generate a meaningful moderation of extremes, with the system's minimal energy load offset by on-site solar."

"The approach places the team at the leading edge of a shift in conservation practice worldwide: moderating extremes rather than chasing a static, museum-standard environment, and weighing the long-term needs of the art against both energy demands and the experiential cost of fully conditioning the space," said Schaum Architects.

The Artillery Sheds will be closed during construction, with the aluminium works removed for the first time since their installation, while the rest of the museum will remain open

Schaum, formerly a principal at Schaun/Shieh before breaking out into his self-named firm, has worked on other buildings related to the late artist, including a recently completed renovation of Judd's architecture office in Marfa.

Judd's New York home and studio was restored by New York office ARO in 2013.

The photography is by Alex Marks.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a restorative infrastructure designed to support eel habitats among projects from the University of Nottingham.

Also featured are artist housing and studios in Hull, and a circular economy materials warehouse in Liverpool.

University of Nottingham

Institution: Architecture and Built Environment
Course: Bachelor of Architecture with Honours in Architecture (ARB/RIBA/LAM Part 1), Master's in Engineering with Honours in Architecture and Environmental Design (CIBSIE and ARB/RIBA/LAM Part 1)
Tutors: Margaret Mulcahy and Alisdair Russell

School statement:

"The Department of Architecture and Built Environment at the University of Nottingham is a leading centre for education and research, preparing future architects, engineers and built-environment professionals to address global challenges.

"Through design innovation, technical excellence and industry engagement, the department advances sustainable buildings, places and communities.

"Sustainability is embedded throughout its teaching and research, equipping graduates to support the transition to net zero and create a more resilient future.

"Building on the department's internationally recognised commitment to sustainability and innovation in the built environment, the Architecture BArch (ARB/RIBA Part 1) is a three-year degree built around thoughtfulness, creativity, individual choice, independent research, critical thinking and technical rigour.

"It is delivered side-by-side with the Architecture and Environmental Design MEng (ARB/RIBA Part 1 and CIBSE), a four-year master's course with an additional year primarily focused on environmental design.

"11 design studios including a live build project in South Africa are structured in five thematic streams – Urban Initiatives, Design and Make, Cultural Contexts, Poetic Narrative and Community.

"Each provides a wide range of opportunities for students to excel in architectural design with a focus on their individual interests and research, supported by modules in architectural humanities, construction and environmental sciences, as illustrated below."

Housing as a System, Not an Object by Faith Spencer

"This project reimagines an underused multi-storey car park in central Milton Keynes as a civic housing factory and public archive.

"Rather than treating housing as a finished product, it explores architecture as part of a wider system of production, education and public engagement.

"The retained concrete structure is transformed into a facility where timber housing components are manufactured, assembled and distributed across the city, while visitors can observe the process through a series of public routes and viewing galleries.

"By making housing production visible, the project aims to reconnect communities with how homes are designed, manufactured and delivered."

Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 1A Forgotten Places
Tutor: Alisdair Russell
Email: faithspencer2005[at]gmail.com

Common Ground by Oyku Kadioglu

"Common Ground is a Soil Research Centre in Lincoln that reconnects people with soil, food and environmental research.

"Visitors follow a journey through the building, beginning in the exhibition, passing visually open laboratories where research can be observed, and ending in the greenhouse where the final outcomes are experienced.

"The project brings together research, education and public engagement while introducing new green spaces and sustainable strategies to create a healthier and more connected urban environment."

Student: Oyku Kadioglu
Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 1B The Janus Condition
Tutors: Jim Hutcheson, Steve Riley, Ben Okrafo-Smart and Alex Lipinski
Email: oykukadioglu04[at]gmail.com

Malesa Daycare Centre by Design and Build Studio

"Since 2009, the Design and Build Studio has delivered more than 12 projects in low-income communities within South Africa, supporting early childhood education for over 4,000 children.

"Through partnerships with the Thušanang Trust and Education Africa, students gain hands-on, project-based learning that integrates design, construction and social engagement.

"The studio is founded on the belief that building is an essential part of learning to design, enabling students to develop practical skills while creating meaningful social impact.

"Over 500 students have participated, contributing to projects that enrich local communities and support their own professional and personal development."

Student: Design+Build Studio
Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 2A Design+Build
Tutors: Pete Russell, Mike Hawkins, Alex Frehse Studio and Aleks Stojakovic

The Current Academy by Nishty Anupchandra

"This current academy challenges the idea that water treatment infrastructure should remain hidden from public view.

"The proposal combines phytoremediation and electrocoagulation within publicly accessible architecture, making the process of water purification visible rather than concealed.

"Bringing together specialised treatment systems, research facilities, educational programmes and public spaces, the academy encourages visitors to engage with the treatment process firsthand.

"The building choreographs the movement of people alongside the movement of water, revealing each stage of purification and its systems are also externally exposed, showing how architecture can communicate complex environmental systems through its spatial experience."

Student: Nishty Anupchandra
Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 2C Adapt/Adept
Tutors: Nils Jaeger, John Ramsay and Craig Smith
Email: nishtykamhal[at]gmail.com

The Parade Gardens by Oliver Hanley

"The Parade Gardens, located in Uxbridge, reimagines a stalled developer-centric apartment block as a community-focused neighbourhood for veterans and military families while cherishing the site's RAF roots.

"In response to the UK's housing crisis and the growing number of empty homes, the project explores adaptive reuse as a compassionate alternative to demolition, transforming forgotten spaces into homes that prioritise people over profit.

"Through generous, high-quality housing, shared community spaces, sustainable retrofit strategies and a strong connection to nature, the proposal aspires to foster belonging, nurture wellbeing and create a long-term, resilient community where new memories can be made."

Student: Oliver Hanley
Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 3A New Ruins
Tutors: Aidan Hall, Cat Mollett, Roz Peebles and Sif Nielsen
Email: oliverhanley44[at]outlook.com

Between Movement and Mooring by Ella Moore

"Between Movement and Mooring responds to the displacement of artists from Hull's Fruit Market development by establishing a new creative community across Humber Dock Marina.

"Inspired by dock movement, the project explores transience and permanence through two artist typologies: temporary prefabricated residences for emerging creatives and permanent live-work studios for established artists.

"Shared workshops bridge both materials and communities, encouraging collaboration and knowledge exchange.

"Public routes, exhibition spaces and waterside connections weave through the scheme, strengthening the relationship between artists, visitors, and Hull's maritime heritage while reactivating the marina as a place of creativity rooted in its industrial history."

Student: Ella Moore
Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 4A Narrative Identities
Tutors: Amanda Harmer and Matt Strong
Email: ellarosemoore05[at]icloud.com

Stewards of the Strata by Hope Yeates

"A former quarry is reawakened as a living archive, where climbing, geology and ecology dissolve the boundaries between adventure, education and stewardship.

"Stewards of the Strata transforms Horseshoe Quarry into a hybrid climbing and geological research centre, combining recreation, scientific research and habitat restoration within a shared landscape.

"Embedded within the quarry, the architecture reuses limestone waste and Sheffield steel to reflect the site's industrial heritage while democratising access to the Peak District through learning, exploration and stewardship."

Student: Hope Yeates
Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 4D Tactile Fictions
Tutor: Sam Critchlow
Email: hopeyeates[at]gmail.com

Mersey Works by Eva Milanta

"Regeneration frequently imports new identities into places that already have one – the Ten Streets needs renewal grounded in what already exists.

"Once powered by the Mersey, this was one of the city's hardest-working industrial landscapes. Mersey Works proposes a circular economy materials warehouse: reclaimed material from across the district enters, is processed and reworked, and re-enters ongoing construction.

"Part workshop, part public experience, making transformation visible. Two routes extend this logic: the adaptive reuse route through heritage structures, and the makers route linking existing workshops into a network of industry and continuity. The district rebuilds itself from its own fabric."

Student: Eva Milanta
Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 5B Nurturing the City
Tutor: Adam Swain-Fossey
Email: evamil2005[at]gmail.com

Recast by Jack Bleazard

"Recast proposes a building that digests buildings, constructing and adapting itself in the process. It represents the last stop on the linear journey of each material imported, rehabilitating demolition waste and exporting re-usable, polyvalent construction units.

"The material re-use hub combines public education, research and productive storage to support the transition towards a nodal economy.

"Located along the Manchester Ship Canal, the scheme challenges perceptions of waste by making re-use visible and accessible.

"The integration of processing workshops with educational facilities equips built environment professionals with the knowledge to implement re-use strategies locally, while elevated walkways exhibit the architectural potential of 'multi-modal materials' to visitors."

Student: Jack Bleazard
Course: Architecture and Environmental Design MEng (Hons), Unit 5C Neighbourhood Ecology
Tutors: Matt Mitchell and Ila Lombardini
Email: jack.bleazard[at]icloud.com

Anguilla: European Eel Conservation and Education Centre by Lily-Grace Conradie

"Anguilla is a landscape-led environmental project that reimagines conservation as a public experience.

"Responding to the critical decline of the European eel, the proposal explores how architecture can become a mediator between ecological recovery and human engagement.

"Through research, education and community interaction, the project reveals the hidden complexities of the river system while creating spaces for restoration, reflection and learning.

"Informed by the eel's extraordinary lifecycle and the barriers that threaten its migration, Anguilla operates as ecological infrastructure – reconnecting habitats, communities and waterways through a shared vision for a more resilient future."

Student: Lily-Grace Conradie
Course: Architecture BArch Hons, Unit 3B Collage Territories
Tutors: Farida Makki and Kathryn Goligher

item.content:encoded:
Stepped, pastel-pink seating spills out from inside the OBA Next Lab library and community space in Amsterdam, designed by Dutch architecture practices Matter Makers, AWR and BAZ Studio as a public living room.

Completed for The Public Library of Amsterdam, or OBA, the 1,175-square-metre timber structure provides a library, cinema, cafe and events space on a previously vacant public square in Amsterdam-Zuidoost.

According to Matter Makers, AWR and BAZ Studio, the building is a response to a "generational shift in how knowledge is shared". It features retractable walls, curtain dividers and movable furniture that allow it to be easily reconfigured.

The project is the latest iteration of a wider project called Next Lab and follows a pilot scheme in Sluisbuurt. After a planned seven-year lifespan, the OBA Next Lab will be dismantled and relocated, enabled by its modular timber structure.

"We reimagined the library for a digital-native generation: less about traditional stacks of books, and more about a vibrant community hub where knowledge is shared in countless ways," Matter Makers founder Antoine van Erp told Dezeen.

"The multifaceted learning spaces are organised around the central atrium, which functions as a living room for the neighbourhood," he added.

OBA Next Lab was constructed from 24 prefabricated, demountable units made of dry-fit panels, columns and beams and raised on foundations of precast slabs to avoid the use of poured concrete.

These exposed timber beams frame a double-height glazed atrium at the heart of the building. Here, a multipurpose pastel-pink "sitting hill" with planters acts as seating for events or reading and extends out into the adjacent square.

Read:

AOR Architects draws on harbour warehouses for Talas community centre in Helsinki

"Central in the design is a giant pink sitting hill. A three-dimensional object that acts as both seating and placemaking, beginning inside the atrium and flowing outward into the public square," Van Erp explained.

"It invites visitors to play on, read in a hidden nook behind some plants, or sit on during a movie screening, lecture or workshop," he added.

An L-shaped block containing the library, work areas and maker spaces overlooks this central atrium through glazed internal walls, with curtains allowing for daylight and visual connections to be mediated.

Externally, the largely glazed ground floor is topped by a band of narrow timber battens and vertical louvres that help to shade the upper level, and the sunken roof has been topped with repurposed photovoltaic cells.

Other community spaces recently featured on Dezeen include the timber Talas community centre in Helsinki by AOR Architects and the adaptable Becontree Estate community hub that Assemble built within a pair of dairy warehouses.

The photography is by Riccardo de Vecchi unless stated otherwise.

item.content:encoded:
Danish amusement park Tivoli has unveiled Hikari, a new area informed by Japanese cities that features art by Takashi Murakami and was designed to be "genuinely respectful of its origin".

The 2,000-square-metre Hikari, which is located in a part of Tivoli that already had a Japanese garden and pagoda, is the latest area at the historic theme park to draw on other parts of the world.

"Tivoli has always looked to the world for inspiration," Tivoli Gardens CEO Susanne Mørch Koch told Dezeen.

"You see it in the Chinese-inspired Pantomime Theatre, the Moorish-inspired Nimb and throughout the Gardens."

"Bringing the world to Copenhagen and interpreting it through Tivoli's own imagination has been part of our DNA for more than 180 years," she continued.

"Japan felt like a natural next chapter. Hikari now lives alongside two existing Japanese-inspired elements in Tivoli: The Pagoda and the gardens around the lake."

The area, which Tivoli says was designed as a "respectful and authentic interpretation of a Japanese district rather than a direct replication", draws on Tokyo, as well as Kyoto and Osaka.

It features Japan-style buildings, shops and Japanese restaurants, as well as the Hotel Hikari fun house.

"It was important to us that the street reflected different periods of Japanese architecture," Tivoli design and development director Rasmus Altenborg told Dezeen.

"We wanted each building to have its own character, while still working together as a kind of patchwork of colours, materials and styles."

The Hikari area also has a new ride, the spinning Typhoon's Eye, which has an exterior that resembles shoji screens.

"When it came to the attractions, space was one of our biggest constraints, so we had to be creative," Altenborg continued.

"We knew we wanted a thrill ride to complement [the existing] The Demon; something exciting to ride, but also spectacular to watch from elsewhere in the Gardens."

To create the buildings in Hikari, Tivoli sourced 60 tonnes of bricks from Japan, as well as 200 wooden windows and doors, sake barrels and kokeshi dolls.

The team worked on the design of the area with an advisory board that included Danish and Danish-Japanese experts, as well as a Japanese graphic designer who also contributed to the signage design.

Among the designs in Hikari – Japanese for light – are Japanese movie posters, depictions of cherry blossoms, kokeshi dolls, pagodas and cats.

Read:

Seven exhibitions that showcased Japanese design in Copenhagen

The design team aimed to make the street feel "rich and alive", Altenborg said.

"The cat, for example, appears in several different forms throughout Hikari," he explained.

"Cats have a long presence in Japanese culture, and today the Maneki-neko cat is one of the most recognisable examples. The cat gradually became a character we grew quite fond of ourselves. We don't really have a cat anywhere else in Tivoli, so it felt like a fun character to make part of Hikari."

The area also has an artwork by Japanese artist Murakami, which depicts a flower and was partly chosen as Tivoli is known for its gardens.

"Takashi Murakami was a particularly interesting choice because his work bridges traditional Japanese visual culture, contemporary art and popular culture," Koch said.

"The smiling flower feels almost made for Tivoli," she continued. "We are, after all, known as an enchanting garden with unique flowers, so there is something very natural and playful about having Murakami's flower become part of our garden."

While amusement parks have a long tradition of depicting buildings from different cultures, creating an area that so fully relies on seemingly typical Japanese designs could be interpreted as exotifying the country.

According to Koch, the amusement park took this into consideration when creating Hikari.

"That distinction has been important to us," she said. "While Hikari is brought together with Tivoli's own architecture and historical tradition, we have spent years developing the area, travelled to Japan, involved Japanese consultants and partners and carefully selected everything from architectural references and artworks to materials and products."

"We did this to ensure the area would be Tivoli's interpretation of Japan but at the same time genuinely respectful of its origin," Koch continued.

"Our ambition was never to build a miniature Japan or claim to represent Japanese culture in its entirety," she added. "Hikari is a Tivoli-interpretation inspired by Japan."

The project, which was five years in the making and opens at a time when there is extensive interest in Japan in Denmark, is Tivoli's most ambitious architectural investment for over 200 years.

The amusement park is betting on it continuing to attract people over decades to come.

"Japan is attracting growing international interest, but the qualities that inspired us: craftsmanship, aesthetics, attention to detail and the interplay between tradition and innovation, have had a much more enduring appeal for Tivoli," Koch concluded.

Previously at Tivoli, BIG released visuals of a pagoda-like hotel for the amusement park. In Seoul, MVRDV incorporated facades of nearby buildings onto the walls of an indoor theme park.

The photography is by Anne-Sophie Rosenvinge.

item.content:encoded:
The Architects Registration Board has announced changes to its professional practice experience approach, which will see its two-year requirement of industry experience scrapped.

Other changes include revisions to the organisation's Standards for learning providers, new guidance for employers and trainees, and a new Trainee Record of Experience process.

The changes form part of the Architects Registration Board's (ARB) wider reforms to its Profession Practice Experience, or PPE. During this, trainees gain experience working in architectural practice, which is required for registration in the UK.

According to the organisation, these changes aim to improve the route to registration by giving trainees "clearer and more consistent support".

New framework to provide "greater transparency for trainees"

Under the new requirements, which are expected to come into force in December 2028, ARB's requirement for applicants to have completed at least two years of practical experience will be scrapped. Instead, timeframes will vary depending on an individual's training and practical experience.

"Our aim is to make sure that all trainees have access to high-quality practical experience and the support they need to develop the competence required for registration," ARB chair Alan Kershaw said.

"The new framework for practical experience published today will give learning providers greater flexibility to integrate academic learning and practical experience," he continued.

"It will also provide much greater transparency for trainees about what they should expect from their PPE and how they can access guidance and support."

In response to concerns over this change reducing the standards required for registration, the ARB has highlighted that applicants will still need qualifications demonstrating that they have met all of ARB's Competency Outcomes.

Read:

"There has not been cultural change as a result of Grenfell" says ARB CEO Hugh Simpson

"The feedback we received through our consultation has helped us further strengthen and refine our proposals," Kershaw said. "We have used this to shape changes that will give trainees a more supportive and flexible experience, while maintaining the high standards required for registration."

Alongside this, the ARB has also published new guidance for trainees and employers outlining their respective roles, and updated its Accreditation Handbook to reflect its revised Standards for learning providers.

Additionally, trainees, learning providers and employers will use a Trainee Record of Experience intended to support "structured reflection" on their practical experience.

The record will not be assessed by the ARB. Instead, it will work to "identify gaps in experience" in order for trainees to meet the required Competency Outcomes and registration.

Rules to take effect from 2028

The announcement by the ARB comes after a year-long review by the organisation in 2025, which examined its Profession Practice Experience.

This was followed by a consultation earlier this year, with the feedback used to inform the proposed changes.

The new rules announced by the ARB will take effect from 31 December 2028, by which point all qualifications must have transitioned to the new framework.

In other ARB news, a recent interview with CEO Hugh Simpson suggested that necessary cultural change within the construction industry is still yet to happen following the devastating Grenfell Tower.

The top image is by Daniel McCullough, courtesy of Unsplash.

item.content:encoded:
Furniture company IKEA has launched the limited-edition Konstrunda collection, an assortment of furniture and homeware objects that reimagine collectible design from the likes of Andu Masebo at an affordable price point.

Konstrunda, or Art Tour, consists of 22 pieces by seven designers, including work from Masebo, Italian designer Emanuele Stamuli and Swedish talents like Lisa Hilland, all for under £200.

"By elevating everyday objects into art pieces, we give people the opportunity to live with art, rather than just viewing it from a distance in a museum," Konstrunda creative leader Karin Gustavsson told Dezeen. "We have the ability to offer this at a price that people can afford."

"Konstrunda can be that entry point for a younger person who is just beginning to collect pieces for the home."

The objects range from a £19 black-and-white vase designed by architect Emanuele Stamuli to Masebo's £149 Konstrunda side table, wrapped in a chunky frame reminiscent of the Tubular Chair that first catapulted him to international attention.

The London designer also contributed two geometric stools that can double as side tables or plinths, one made of raw pine and the other covered in bright blue paint.

The IKEA collaboration marks Masebo's latest foray into low-cost mass production following his show at Unit.d gallery in London, where he created affordable, everyday objects from folded sheet metal.

"Scalability has always been something I've been interested in engaging with. I want to make work that is rich in depth, but I also want it to be felt by people outside of my own bubble."

"To make something that can be considered art, that can also be accessible is a really interesting challenge to consider," he told Dezeen.

Swedish artist Lisa Reiser created mouthblown glass vases informed by her own daydreams for the collection, including a bright-green "gummy candy" version, while Hilland contributed a pinewood stool and a bent orange sculpture.

Designers Ingrid Leander and Igor Holtermann worked together on boldly patterned cushions and a rug informed by zebra crossings and caution banners they observed in the Stockholm streetscape.

Read:

"IKEA has challenged the rest of the design world"

In-house designer Akanksha Deo hoped to address the contemporary loneliness epidemic with two expressive vessels, one of which resembles a "character" made of stacked blocks to give people a sense of companionship.

Despite their functionality, Gustavsson refers to all of the pieces in the collection as "art objects", since she says the furniture giant doesn't see "art and design as separate worlds".

"This brief was about artistic expression, not about beginning with a functional need or everyday challenge that needed to be solved," said Gustavsson.

"We at IKEA feel that collectible design shouldn't have a barrier to entry, that to collect things you love and that speak to you should be available for the many."

IKEA also recently released its 2026 PS collection, which is similarly playful and affordable. Writer Debika Ray recently explored the impact of the collection, while Dezeen discussed if the price point was "too good to be true" on a recent podcast.

item.content:encoded:
International studio Open Architecture drew on Lina Bo Bardi's own designs when creating The Poetics of Survival, the first major exhibition of the architect's work in China.

The studio centred the exhibition, which is on show at the Power Station of Art (PSA) gallery in Shanghai, around "a single continuous curve".

This shape was created by using hanging linen curtains in the rectangular art gallery, where they surround rectilinear display cases custom-made by Open Architecture.

In PSA's lobby, the studio created a replica of the indoor pond designed by Bardi for the SESC Pompéia community centre in 1977, though they didn't make it as permanent as the original.

"In Lina's version, the pond embodies the São Francisco River, which runs across Brazil," the studio said.

"It was 'transported' to Shanghai at its original scale. However, in the PSA gallery, it is not embedded into the ground as it does at SESC Pompéia, but instead, appears to levitate slightly above the ground surface."

Read:

"Experience of Brasília" evoked at interior installation in Niemeyer's São Paulo pavilion

To add interest, Open Architecture filled the pond with pebbles in a variety of sizes and added a water feature that sees water drip from the ceiling.

In the main exhibition spaces, the studio created freestanding "islands" for the architectural models and other key exhibition pieces.

The exhibition was divided into nine spaces, which highlight Bardi's work through a mix of media – including sketches, photographs and videos.

The Poetics of Survival features large-scale projections that move across the linen curtains, creating a dynamic feel, and the exhibition texts are also silkscreen-printed directly onto the linen.

As well as the display cabinets, Open Architecture custom-made some furniture pieces for the space, including a bench made from wooden beams and a glass, latticed wood and concrete divider in the lobby.

The studio hoped that the design for The Poetics of Survival will give visitors a feel for what inspired Bardi.

"Presenting Lina's work within a setting that is informed by her own design ethos and sensibility allows audiences to encounter not only her work, but also get a sense of the world that inspired it," Open Architecture said.

"Therefore, Lina's work and the exhibition, together, become a stage where the audience get a glimpse of the everyday reality of Brazil in Lina's time."

Other recent exhibitions include a contemporary design show in a neo-gothic house in Belgium and an exhibition about Brasília set within Oscar Niemeyer's Bienal Pavilion in São Paulo.

The photography is by Chen Hao, courtesy of Open Architecture.

The Poetics of Survival is on show at The Power Station of Art, 678 Miaojiang Road, Huangpu District, Shanghai, China 200011 from July 25 to October 25 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
The New York office of OMA and local practice YA Studio have arranged a 160-home apartment block in San Francisco, California, around multiple courtyards.

Named 730 Stanyan, the development is OMA's first 100 per cent affordable housing complex in the United States.

Set near Golden Gate Park and the famous Haight-Ashbury neighbourhood, the block was developed for the Chinatown Community Development Center (CNDC) and Tenderloin Neighborhood Development Corporation (TNDC) .

The building rises to eight storeys with a central block that has a light facade colouration.

Two four-storey envelopes bookend the structure, in order to better relate to the scale of the neighbourhood, said OMA and YA Studio.

It was clad in a "series of modular GFRC 'wave' panels" according to the studio, which were "shaped to playfully echo the rhythm and form of the neighborhood's townhomes".

The panels also provide technical elements such as integrated windows and ventilation louvres. Fabricated at different lengths to cross the differing spans of the facade they curve around the courtyard spaces cut into the building.

"By carving 730 Stanyan to maximize light, views, and shared outdoor spaces, we sought to create homes that are generous and deeply connected to the surrounding community and Golden Gate Park," said OMA partner-in-charge Jason Long.

This method allowed for the building to have three ground-level courtyards, one facing the street in a deep, U-shaped entrance courtyard, while the other two are more square and abut the neighbouring building.

Each courtyard was designed by local studio GLS Landscape Architecture.

The entrance courtyard opens onto the park across the street, with glazing along the ground floor in this section to bring light into the passageway connecting gathering spaces and other amenities.

OMA's industrial style comes out in the gridded metal ceiling plates that cover the circulation and public areas.

The block's angular exterior was designed in part to maximise both space for internal apartments and openness to the outside.

More than 50 per cent of homes are two- and three-bedroom apartments, facilitating family dwelling.

"Maximizing the number of corners allowed OMA and YA Studio to plan efficient apartments that provide generous homes, many with views to the park," said the team.

Read:

OMA designs pyramidal building in China as "three-dimensional village"

Having two different heights in the structures also allowed for patios on top of the four-storey blocks.

Inside, the apartments are characterised by high ceilings and simple detailing.

Throughout the private and public spaces, circular concrete structural columns were left exposed to become part of the interior architecture.

Other renowned studios that have made an entrance into affordable housing include Herzog & de Meuron's design for a housing block in New York and social housing by Studio Libeskind in Brooklyn.

The photography is by Jason O'Rear.

item.content:encoded:
The Thompson Center in downtown Chicago has been given a new facade as part of a renovation for tech company Google by architecture studio Jahn.

Photos taken earlier this month show the largely complete facade of the Thompson Center, which is in the midst of a complete overhaul by Jahn.

Originally designed in the 1980s by Jahn founder Helmut Jahn, the building was considered one of the most significant pieces of post-modern architecture in the USA.

Built for the Illinois state government and named after former Illinois governor James R Thompson, the building was under threat of demolition after plans to sell it were made public in 2015.

In 2022, the building was sold to Google's parent company Alphabet Inc, which decided to undertake a thorough renovation.

The building is set to become Google's Chicago HQ with office space on the upper floors and shops and restaurants on the lower floors.

As part of the renovation, the original, slightly darkened patterned glass that wrapped the building has been replaced by a sleek, uniform curtain wall.

This triple-glazed facade forms part of the strategy to greatly improve the environmental performance of the building.

Read:

Helmut Jahn's postmodern Thompson Center saved from demolition

While renderings released ahead of the renovation showed a transparent facade with clear views into the building from the street, the photos appear to show a reflective finish on the glazing.

Below the sloped, glass facade, the photos show a concrete and brass colonnade that replaced the original red and beige stone finishes.

The renovation of the highly distinctive building will also see the building's central, 17-storey atrium overhauled.

Renderings of the space, which is expected to be open to the public, show a stepped, circular space with restaurants, cafes and workspaces.

The renovation is planned to be completed in 2027, with the building's name changed from the James R Thompson Center to the Thompson Center.

The building was the most famous work designed by long-time Chicago resident Helmut Jahn, who died in a bicycle crash aged 81 in 2021.

The photography is by Tom Ravenscroft.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a project aiming to optimise architect Berthold Lubetkin's Grade I-listed Finsbury Health Centre for 21st-century users is among those by the University of Nottingham.

Also included are a scheme for a sustainability-centric primary school to encourage eco-conscious habits in children, and an urban regeneration plan for a historic high street in Norwich, UK.

University of Nottingham

Institution: University of Nottingham
School: Department of Architecture and Built Environment
Courses: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2), L7 Apprenticeship, MArch Sustainable Urban Design, MArch Advanced Architecture Design, and MArch Architecture and Sustainable Design
Tutors: Graeme Barker, Tim Collett, Amy Tang, Tim Heath, Lorna Kiamba, Renata Tubelo and Lucelia Rodrigues

School statement:

"The Department of Architecture and Built Environment at the University of Nottingham is a leading centre for education and research, preparing future architects, engineers and built-environment professionals to address global challenges.

"Building on a strong reputation for sustainability and innovation, the department offers a range of postgraduate programmes spanning architecture, sustainable design, environmental engineering, building performance and urban development.

"These combine academic excellence with practical application, equipping students with advanced technical expertise, problem-solving skills and a strong foundation in sustainability, as illustrated in the examples below.

"MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2) gives students the skills to become successful and employable architects. It is shaped around six core themes: sustainability, continuity, construction, urban transformation, social inclusivity, and inhabitation.

"MArch Sustainable Urban Design equips students with the design, research, and strategic planning skills needed to create sustainable, resilient and inclusive urban environments.

"MArch Advanced Architecture Design enables students to pursue contemporary agendas that address critical challenges within the built environment from a research-led design perspective.

"MArch Architecture and Sustainable Design integrates architecture with environmental performance and sustainable technologies, equipping students with design skills that respond to contemporary challenges."

Unbuilding Trent Basin: A Circular Resource Hub by Anthony Tse

"Unbuilding Trent Basin reimagines the existing city as a material repository rather than a landscape of obsolete structures.

"By transforming redundant warehouses into centres for urban mining, material exchange and collective making, the project treats the city itself as a resource bank rather than a site of continual extraction and replacement.

"Land liberated from storage and waste functions is gradually returned to productive landscapes, while reclaimed materials are recirculated into future construction.

"As a prototype for degrowth urbanism, the project challenges expansion-led development and demonstrates how cities can prosper through repair, reuse, and collective care."

Student: Anthony Tse
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Alison Davies and Richard Woods
Email: anthonytse98[at]gmail.com

City Commoning by Bethany Humphrey

"High street decline is an existential threat to communities in urban centres, who rely on them as critical social infrastructure ecosystems.

"This design includes a series of retrofits to vacant commercial units, temporary pavilions, and a green street pedestrianisation strategy along Norwich's historic Magdalen Street, an ecosystem at risk of being overwhelmed by residential expansion.

"These include a redundant medieval church adapted into a young enterprise hub, a former antiques emporium transformed into a youth centre, and a prefabricated market under St Crispin's Flyover.

"The social capital of the whole is greater than the sum of each space."

Student: Bethany Humphrey
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Tim Collett and Naomi Eckworth
Email: b.humphrey01[at]gmail.com

Architecture and Energy: A Self-Sustaining Sports Complex by Cecil Pun

"The thesis explores sustainability through the relationship between architecture and energy, informed by the theory of 'form follows fuel' – the idea that architectural form is shaped by dominant energy systems available to society.

"As we transition towards decarbonisation, the form must also evolve. The project reimagines Greenwich Power Station, a product of fossil fuel, as a self-sustaining sports complex that generates, stores, and conserves its own energy.

"Its environmental strategy prioritises passive design, renewable energy, and adaptable spaces that respond to seasonal change, reducing energy demand while reconnecting occupants with natural environmental conditions."

Student: Cecil Pun
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Tim Collett and Naomi Eckworth
Email: cecilpun[at]gmail.com

Tooting Exchange: Architecture Beyond Consumption by Emily Gibson

"Tooting Exchange offers a civic alternative to the contemporary high street.

"Set within the dense commercial fabric of Tooting Market, the project turns underused space into a setting for everyday participation, repair, learning and exchange.

"Instead of adding another consumption driven destination, it creates a porous social landscape that encourages lingering, gathering and informal occupation.

"Existing structures are kept and adapted over time, reducing embodied carbon while preserving the site's memory and identity.

"The project explores how architecture can give spatial form to principles of degrowth, sufficiency, conviviality, participation and collective wellbeing through adaptable civic infrastructure woven into the rhythms of the high street."

Student: Emily Gibson
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2) Level 7 Apprenticeship
Tutors: Nick Haynes and Paula Schilliger
Email: emily-gibson10[at]hotmail.co.uk

Agency of the Void: Between Institution and City by Evlin Servis

"Exploring how architecture can reconnect institutions with public life, the thesis proposes a hybrid civic-cultural institution on a residual wharf in Bristol, positioned between St Mary Redcliffe and the Floating Harbour.

"The scheme acts as a civic centre and extension to Bristol's existing Urban Room, using overlapping public interiors and layered thresholds to draw movement through the site, re-intensify the route between the city and St Mary Redcliffe and create a more legible and inhabitable public landscape.

"Through a pedestrianised urban realm, activated canal frontage and public cut-throughs, the scheme establishes a new urban promenade reconnecting communities and supporting regeneration."

Student: Evlin Servis
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Alison Davies and Richard Woods
Email: evlinservis[at]gmail.com

ReSource by Matthew James

"The architectural profession today finds itself at the intersection between two revolutions: a digital revolution threatening the agency of the maker, and an environmental one demanding a shift in our attitude toward material consumption.

"ReSource investigates the paradox between craftsmanship and circularity through the transformation of the soon-to-be-demolished Colechurch House, unlocking the huge material potential of an unloved building.

"This model exhibits 'Connective Craft' – part of the existing building is transformed: an extension structure is formed with steel from an existing bridge, removed concrete is stacked to form columns, and the precast cladding is rotated to create new shading."

Student: Matthew James
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Kate Nicklin and Graham Mateer
Email: matthew.t.james.studio[at]gmail.com

Catalyst Works by Oliver Roberts

"The Catalyst Works is an urban quarry for recovering, processing and redistributing architectural materials within the regeneration of Frog Island, Leicester.

"With regeneration understood as a time dependent process, the project is structured through three strategies – Permanence, Adaptability and Temporary Activation – allowing regeneration to occur incrementally through phased occupation and evolving use.

"Permanent interventions preserve embodied value and establish civic infrastructure, adaptable systems support long-term change, and temporary interventions catalyse early occupation and material reuse.

"Together, these strategies demonstrate how architecture can enable resilient, low-impact regeneration through circular material flows and incremental transformation."

Student: Oliver Roberts
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Kate Nicklin and Graham Mateer
Email: oj.roberts[at]yahoo.com

The Learning Grove by Gopika Pillai Deepu

"This sustainable primary school reimagines learning by shaping spaces that inspire children to discover, play and grow.

"The building is designed to reduce carbon emissions and encourage eco-conscious habits through solar integration, green mobility and creating environmental awareness.

"The design was supported by evidence-based tools such as IESVE, PHPP and Sefaira, ensuring strong environmental performance.

"Guided by RIBA sustainable outcomes, every space enhances daylight, air quality, and thermal comfort while maintaining a close connection to nature.

"Inclusive, accessible, and energy-efficient, the school becomes a living classroom where children learn to live lightly and grow toward a greener future."

Student: Gopika Pillai Deepu
Course: MArch Architecture and Sustainable Design
Tutors: Lorna Kiamba and Renata Tubelo
Email: ar.gopikapillai01[at]gmail.com

Therme Hill by Mithilesh Rani

"Therme Hill answers the question 'what if nature shaped urban health?' by anchoring memory, wellness and the vitality of living beside a 'hill', within a tropical wellness precinct.

"Situated along the quiet edge of the Bridgewater Canal in Trafford Park, the design counters industrial zoning and a harsh microclimate by enclosing a warm, tropical sanctuary beneath a monumental free-form grid shell while extending Manchester's green belt with a dense plantation.

"Integrating stalactite-inspired structural columns, suspended vegetation, family pools, an indoor beach and community farming, the project vitalises social sustainability by catalysing public access to nature in the city."

Student: Mithilesh Rani
Course: MArch Advanced Architecture Design
Tutors: Amy Tang, Tim Heath and Anran Chen
Email: laxmr10[at]nottingham.ac.uk

Reimagining Finsbury Health Centre: Architecture for Health by Aidan Sinclair

"This thesis reimagines the Grade I listed Finsbury Health Centre, extending Berthold Lubetkin's vision of public welfare for the 21st century.

"Rooted in the building's original commitment to collective wellbeing, the proposal transforms the site into a contemporary health and wellbeing district.

"Alongside primary healthcare services, the scheme introduces community programmes, exhibition spaces, and improved public realm.

"New civic spaces strengthen connections between local institutions, integrating healthcare, culture, and every day public life to reduce the stigma of accessing health services.

"Adaptive reuse preserves its heritage and supports future healthcare needs, demonstrating architecture's role in promoting public health and community cohesion."

Student: Aidan Sinclair
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2) Level 7 Apprenticeship
Tutors: Nick Haynes and Paula Schilliger
Email: aidan_sinclair[at]outlook.com

item.content:encoded:
A brick cube reminiscent of old industrial structures forms this family home in the suburbs of Ghent, designed by Belgian architecture studio Atelier Vens Vanbelle.

Named Project Tomas & Katrien after its clients, but nicknamed The Factory by its neighbours, the cubic brick home was disguised as an industrial structure to help create the impression that it had "always been there", the studio said.

"We proposed to the city services to build our home against a large blind wall on the property boundary to neatly close off the row of houses, but the city did not want to go along with this idea," Atelier Vens Vanbelle told Dezeen.

"We were required to build a detached house. Therefore, we chose to design a brick building that refers to old industrial or workshop architecture, so that it creates the impression of having always been there."

Project Tomas & Katrien comprises two storeys organised around a central diamond-shaped skylight and light well, which features a lush green planter at its base and is traversed via a bright yellow staircase.

The beams of the home's ground-floor ceiling, as well as its paved and timber-plank floors, have all been positioned to align with this central void, setting them at diagonals to the edges of the home.

This 45-degree angle was also the basis of a diagonal wall on the ground floor that separates the large living, dining and kitchen area from a series of smaller service areas.

Upstairs, the home's four bedrooms are organised around a cross-shaped, multipurpose area that was designed to feel like an extension of the living area below, which it overlooks from behind a bright yellow balustrade.

Read:

Bricolage uses salvaged bricks for self-build home in London

"We wanted to avoid building a traditional home with a living area on the ground floor and an upper floor where there is hardly anything to do. We chose to build a home that can be experienced across both floors," the studio said.

"The 45-degree angle in the floor plan creates a captivating perspective, making the spaces feel even larger than they actually are."

"The materials evoke the atmosphere of an old workshop – bricks combined with old clay tiles, wooden walls and ceilings, and metal stairs and balustrades," added Atelier Vens Vanbelle.

"The palette is raw, yet feels homely and familiar at the same time."

At the end of the home's garden, a garden store is flanked by a bike shelter and seating area. It features perforated brick walls and is covered by a raised, sloping timber and polycarbonate roof.

Elsewhere in Ghent, local architecture studios Atelier Avondzon and Macadam Atelier also looked to industrial structures for their renovation of a derelict home, which features a sawtooth roof and corrugated metal cladding, while Decancq Vercruysse recently reorganised a mid-century bungalow around a fireplace.

The photography is courtesy of Atelier Vens Vanbelle.

item.content:encoded:
The Barbican Centre shop has launched a homeware collection with online retailer Made.com, which includes furniture and lighting modelled on details of the brutalist housing complex in central London.

Geometric, gridded and curved architectural references feature throughout the 23-piece MADE x Barbican homeware collection, which also includes textiles and accessories.

According to the Barbican, the collection was developed following research into the original Barbican Estate apartment layouts, including the work of designer Miriam Howitt, who created five show homes for the estate in the 1960s.

The pieces are designed to be used together or independently and prices start from £32.

"The ambition was to create a complete product range that works both in isolation and together in an open living space," said the Made.com team.

"The final designs reimagine products, graphics and architectural details through a new lens, and into a cohesive product range that captures Barbican living: bold, considered and inherently social."

The Barbican Estate was designed by Chamberlin, Powell and Bon in the 1950s and opened in 1982. It is one of the largest examples of post-war brutalist architecture in the UK.

Within it is the Barbican Centre – an arts and culture venue with theatres, galleries, cinemas, as well as a conservatory, a library and eateries.

A pair of stand-out pieces in the collection is the Curve Table Lamp and Curve Floor Lamp, which have adjustable, tubular shades that draw on the acoustic panels in the Barbican's concert hall.

The lights have chrome bases, with shades available in burgundy, green and blue, contrasted by their fabric cables.

Other lighting pieces include the Coffer ceiling lights and wall lights, which mimic the estate's iconic waffle ceilings, seen throughout its indoor and outdoor spaces.

Furniture pieces in the range include the Dual chairs, with statement side panels made of wood and modelled on the estate's concrete pillars, and the modular Plinth coffee table that echoes the sunken seating next to the Barbican lake.

Other furniture pieces include a dining table and chairs, two sofas, and shelving and storage.

Read:

Takero Shimazaki Architects infuses Barbican flat with Japanese details

Among the accessories is the Brute Rug, which takes visual cues from an original show flat designed by Howitt in 1967, in which she paired plain off-white flats with bold patterned carpets.

It is made from hand-tufted wool with a long shag pile, which the team said was intended "to deliver a retro feel".

The final pieces in the collection are a series of cushions and textile wall art, each depicting the facades and elevations from the estate.

Warm, neutral tones including mossy greens and rusty oranges are used throughout the collection for a mid-century look, contrasted with stained ash and chrome accents.

To celebrate the launch, Made.com will be curating an installation at the Barbican Centre from 12 September that both showcases the collection and interiors of homes at the Barbican.

Other Barbican news recently featured on Dezeen includes the upcoming revamp of the complex by British architecture studios Allies and Morrison and Asif Khan Studio, and a 30-tonne earthen installation at the estate by Delcy Morelos, which was informed by a mother's womb.

The photography is by Felix Speller.
