item.content:encoded:
Local architecture studio Mosley Thorold has updated and extended a Victorian home in east London, using a textured palette of concrete, brick, tiles and metal intended to patina over time.

Named De Beauvoir Townhouse after the neighbourhood in which it is located, Mosley Thorold renovated the two-storey home and added a rear extension that reorients its layout towards a generous garden.

"So many of these houses prioritise the front elevation, the arrival, the public face, inherently – it's all about curb appeal," co-founder Nathan Mosley told Dezeen.

"We wanted to turn that logic inward, so that the garden becomes the primary event rather than an afterthought glimpsed from the back windows," he added.

Two key spatial gestures defined the project. The first was the repositioning of the home's staircase to the rear of the home, where it borrows light and views from a full-height window next to a library with raised ceilings.

The second is a large kitchen and dining area specifically requested by the client for large gatherings, which is organised around a custom dining table designed by Mosley Thorold. This room opens out onto the garden patio via a set of folding doors made from reclaimed shutters.

Steel columns and beams painted a deep reddish-brown frame the extension's interiors, designed as part of a structure to support the formwork of its poured concrete walls without putting strain on the existing party wall.

The tactility of this rough concrete has been complemented externally by weathered metal window frames, and internally by timber ceilings and a checkered floor made from reclaimed cement tiles.

Read:

Will Gamble Architects adds "explicitly tropical" extension to Grade-II listed English cottage

For the living spaces, bedrooms and bathrooms on the home's upper floors, this palette has been translated into walls painted in earthy shades, dark wood floors and concrete basins.

"We wanted materials with an inviting, tactile quality, things you want to touch, as much as look at, but equally we were thinking long term about how they'd age," Mosley said.  "Materials that develop a patina rather than simply wear out."

"Victorian buildings were crafted by hand, and there's a real celebration of what materials could do embedded in that era of building," Mosley added.

"I think contemporary design can carry the same spirit, even if the tools have changed entirely."

Mosley Thorold worked with garden designer Sophie Gordon for the home's garden, which steps up from the lower patio to a lawn lined by salvaged brick beds for planting.

Perpendicular to the main garden, a formerly underutilised strip of land has also been transformed with a natural swimming pool, overlooked by a sauna and changing area finished in rough stone and black timber.

Elsewhere in De Beauvoir, interiors firm Irenie Studio recently collaborated with architect Studio Dera to update a 19th-century townhouse, while Architecture For London added a light-filled extension to a Victorian home.

The photography is by Ollie Tomlinson.

item.content:encoded:
Spanish studio Typsa Arquitectura has completed a library in Luanda, Angola, with a curving concrete roof punctured by openings that encircle existing trees on the site.

Located at the centre of Luanda's technology park, the 1,915-square-metre library was designed around the site's existing mature trees, which determined its footprint, spatial organisation and roof design.

Rather than clearing the plot, Typsa Arquitectura organised the library around a series of planted courtyards, allowing the existing trees to become part of the design.

"Across cultures and throughout history, the shade of a tree has provided a natural place for gathering, learning, exchange and rest," lead architect Marina González Suárez told Dezeen.

"The mature trees became the project's primary design generator," added Suárez.

"Instead of defining the building first and adapting the landscape afterwards, the architecture grew around them."

The library is capped by a curving concrete roof that swells and narrows across the site before opening into circular voids that frame the retained trees.

Supported by a structural system of reinforced concrete slabs and slender steel columns, the roof extends beyond the glazed facades to create deep shaded walkways and broad cantilevers.

Typsa Arquitectura said the trees informed the placement of the courtyards and the building's fluid plan, which replaces conventional corridors with gently curving circulation routes that loop around the planted spaces.

The roof also forms the centrepiece of the library's passive environmental strategy. Separated from the occupied spaces below, it is a ventilated double-layered roof that allows air to circulate continuously, dissipating heat before it reaches the interiors.

Read:

Snøhetta creates library to emulate feeling of "sitting under a tree"

Together with cross-ventilation and the shade provided by the trees, the roof reduces solar gain and helps to create a cooler environment.

The curved glass facades are shaded by tall, adjustable brise soleil screens that pivot according to the sun's orientation.

The brise soleil fins are made of lacquered aluminium and give the elevations a slightly irregular texture.

According to the studio, this system reinterprets the brise soleil commonly found in Angolan modernist architecture, while filtering daylight to cast shifting grid-like shadows across the library's curved white interiors.

Inside, white walls, polished floors and floor-to-ceiling glazing create bright, open interiors animated by shifting shadows cast through the perforated screens.

The library is organised across two public floors, with an additional technical level dedicated to building services.

Visitors enter at ground level, where the main entrance leads into reading areas, administrative offices and a multipurpose auditorium.

A broad central timber staircase ascends to the upper floor, where the principal reading room extends onto a terrace overlooking the surrounding park.

"The sequence of spaces has been designed to encourage an intuitive and relaxed experience," said project director Joaquin Beltran Del Corral.

"Rather than following a linear route, visitors move through a series of interconnected environments that gradually reveal different views, scales and activities."

Founded in Madrid in 1966, Typsa Arquitectura is the architecture division of engineering consultancy Typsa. The practice designs civic, educational, transport and infrastructure projects across Europe, Africa and the Middle East.

Another library designed to emulate the feeling of sitting under a tree is Beijing City Library in China, featuring towering tree-like columns.

Also recently featured on Dezeen was The MAAK's Rahmah Library in Cape Town, where bricks made from Apartheid-era demolition rubble were incorporated into the building.

The photography is by Flavio Ricardo Gomes Cardoso.

item.content:encoded:
A study has found that children living in Star Homes, a housing initiative in Tanzania, have lower rates of malaria, diarrhoea and respiratory infections compared to those living in mud-and-thatch houses.

The study, which was published in Nature Medicine, found that cases of malaria in children were 44 per cent lower for children residing in Star Home residences, diarrhoea was 30 per cent less and acute respiratory infections were reduced by 18 per cent.

The research also found that children living in Star Homes had greater height-for-age growth trajectories, indicating a reversal of stunting, which is a consequence of repeated childhood infection.

Star Homes was designed by representatives of the Royal Danish Academy, which also co-authored the study, in collaboration with Tanzanian and international researchers.

The study was carried out over three years by Tanzanian research group CSK Research Solutions, Tanzania's Ifakara Health Institute, the Mahidol-Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit at the University of Oxford, Durham University in the UK, Amsterdam University Medical Center, University of the Philippines Manila and East, Central and Southern Africa Health Community.

Taking place between January 2022 and December 2024, it looked at children under the age of 13 living across 70 villages in rural Mtwara, Tanzania.

Through a randomised public lottery of over 14,600 surveyed homes, a group of children living in 110 Star Homes was compared to children living in 513 traditional mud-and-thatch houses.

In the study, researchers argued that the contraction of the three preventable yet deadly diseases – malaria, diarrhoea and respiratory infections – is closely linked to the home environment, where children spend a large portion of their days.

It highlighted poor ventilation, overcrowding, poor sanitation and insufficient access to clean water as contributing to the spread of pathogens and airborne infections in the home.

Designed by the Royal Danish Academy in collaboration with Tanzanian and international researchers, Star Homes houses have a two-storey prefabricated structure that uses passive engineering strategies to help with disease prevention.

Bedrooms are positioned on the upper floor to avoid mosquitoes, which are more commonly found at ground level.

Net walls let air in and help with cross-ventilation, keeping sleeping areas cool while keeping mosquitoes out, and screened windows and self-closing doors further prevent insects from entering.

The houses have solar-powered lighting and are built atop an elevated, easy-to-clean concrete floor. Rainwater harvesting provides safe drinking water, a cooking stove vents smoke to the outdoors, and the toilet is a fly-proof, ventilated latrine.

Read:

Architectural Pioneering Consultants and Wolfgang Rossbauer use local materials for a school in Tanzania

"What is groundbreaking about the project is that architecture is incorporated as an active component of a randomised clinical trial and measured with the same level of rigour as medical research," said Star Homes architect and Royal Danish Academy dean Jakob Brandtberg Knudsen.

"What is crucial to our research is not architecture alone, but the interdisciplinary collaboration between architects, social scientists, physicians, biologists, and statisticians," he continued.

"Architecture can function as a health intervention on a par with medicine when it is developed and documented using scientific methods, while at the same time saving resources and reducing carbon emissions."

According to the study, the material cost of a Star Homes house is 24 per cent less than a typical single-storey cement-block house, and it generates 57 per cent less embodied carbon.

The study's authors described it as "the first-ever randomised controlled trial using a house as an intervention", and hope it encourages the building of disease-preventative, low-carbon homes across Africa.

"Our ground-breaking study shows that building better can turn a dangerous home into a safe one by protecting children in sub-Saharan Africa against three major killer diseases," said study author Steve Lindsay, professor of biosciences at Durham University.

"Based on decades of research, this was the first clinical trial of a purpose-built healthy house, and the findings are very exciting," he continued.

"We now hope that the building industry will adopt some of the important features of our healthy house design that are protective, cheaper and use less carbon than conventional concrete African houses."

Other projects in Tanzania that have featured on Dezeen include a school made from local materials, which won architecture project of the year in Dezeen Awards 2023, and a school arranged around a tree-filled courtyard.

The photography is by Julien Lanoo and the video is by Sava Films.

item.content:encoded:
Interior design practice Busta Studio has filled the Kimpton Ashbel hotel on Park Avenue with art and objects intended to make it feel like "a warm, elegantly curated home".

Located in a 1928 beaux-arts building on New York City's famous Park Avenue, Kimpton Ashbel was designed to feel like a private residence.

"Park Avenue is one of New York City's most iconic streets, instantly evoking the elegance of its heritage townhouses," Busta Studio founder Anna Busta told Dezeen.

"Drawing from this distinctive spirit, we envisioned a conceptual townhouse experience – welcoming guests into a warm, elegantly curated home."

Anna and her husband Jonathan Busta, who run Busta Studio together, used hand-brushed blonde limed oak panelling and arches juxtaposed with Bianco Dolomiti and Pietra marbles to create the right feel for the interior.

The studio also combined hand-cast bronze, glass, inlaid bronze and hand-cut mosaic stone with white plaster ceilings and mouldings for a deliberately simple yet elegant look.

"The New York townhouse concept itself is an endless source of inspiration: a place where one lingers, surrounded by bespoke millwork, refined finishes, stylish furnishings, and a curated mix of art and collected objects that feel personal and storied," Jonathan Busta told Dezeen.

To create privacy from the bustle of Park Avenue, custom louvres were added at street level.

Guests are welcomed by a custom inlaid mosaic featuring the hotel's KA initials when entering the lobby, which Busta Studio filled with specially commissioned artworks and decorative objects.

Read:

A-nrd designs Arthouse Glasgow hotel to "feel like it belongs to the city"

"We curated the art collection to create a nice, easy vibe for the interior, with a mixture of graphics, original paintings, photography and sculpture," Anna Busta said.

"All pieces are specifically commissioned for the space, and the overall collection has a simple but sophisticated guiding aesthetic," she continued. "We didn't want to provoke with art, but instead we simply embraced beauty."

The designers wanted to tie the communal spaces and guestrooms at Kimpton Ashbel together by using a coherent colour palette for the hotel, which focuses on calming neutral hues juxtaposed with jewel colours.

"Jewel tones inject vibrancy into accent pieces like arch chairs, side stools, headboards, and art chairs, striking a harmonious balance between subtle and bold statements that add warmth and approachability to the space," Jonathan Busta said.

To create a homely feeling, Busta Studio used velvets, linens, naturally tanned leathers and boucle fabrics.

The studio said it hoped that the mix of tactile materials, refined finishes and well-considered artworks would create a feeling that is reminiscent of a well-designed home.

"We believe the guest experience is enhanced by this intimate approach," Anna Busta concluded.

Other hotels recently featured on Dezeen include a Glasgow hotel in a 19th-century townhouse and a Tokyo boutique hotel designed to feel like staying at the home of a friend.

The photography is courtesy of Kimpton Ashbel.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: atmospherically dark glass and seamless surfaces take centre stage in appliance brand Fisher & Paykel's Minimal Style kitchen products, designed to help build spaces with visual calm and formal rigour.

The Minimal appliances are one of three product design styles in Fisher & Paykel's luxury range, alongside Contemporary and Professional offerings.

The Minimal kitchen line includes handle- and dial-free ovens and flush-fitting cooktops, all designed with the same aim: to sit quietly within the kitchen and support continuous surface planes.

The Minimal appliances are set in contrast to the more expressive lines, brushed silver glass finish and defined controls of the Contemporary range. Together, both are designed to bring the "beauty of choice" to architects, designers and homeowners in the luxury market, according to Fisher & Paykel.

For the Minimal range, the New Zealand company focused not just on simplicity but the deeper formal goals of minimalism, applying scrutiny to "every line, proportion, material junction and surface transition" to reach an essential expression.

At the same time, its designers aspired to beauty, seeking to find poetry in the relationships between surfaces, finishes, light and shadow.

"As kitchens have become more central to the architecture of the home, expectations around integration and refinement have continued to evolve," said Fisher & Paykel head of industrial design (cooking) Adam Moody.

"Advances in materials, connectivity and manufacturing precision are allowing minimalist principles to be realised with new levels of precision and sophistication."

Fisher & Paykel's vision for the Minimal Style kitchen involves combining its ovens, hobs and complementary luxury cooking appliances with integration, concealing refrigeration, wine and dishwashing solutions behind cabinetry to build a calm and cohesive space.

To make the visible appliances contribute to the aesthetic, they are made of black or grey glass, giving them both an atmospheric presence and a sense that they are fading into the background. This also gives designers more freedom to explore colour, material and texture elsewhere in the space.

Seamless finishes are also prioritised, with flush installation, very fine two-millimetre perimeter gaps and designs that are free of handles or dials that would otherwise disrupt the surface plane.

"Where appliances remain visible, the visually recessive qualities of the style extend the intention of integration," said Moody. "It's an approach that draws on enduring principles of minimalist architecture and industrial design: find the essence of an object, then celebrate its form and tactility."

The designers have paid attention to detail to heighten the luxury quality of the products, including elements such as the movement of the oven door, the precise edge detailing and a picture-frame effect giving depth to the oven front.

Large, high-resolution touchscreen displays are designed for responsiveness, while voice control enables easy multitasking, and integration with the SmartHQ connected-home platform allows for remote control and monitoring.

Fisher & Paykel's Minimal Style is available in a range of steam assist, combination steam and convection ovens in 60- and 76-centimetre formats. Companion products like warming drawers, vacuum drawers for sous-vide preparation, and integrated coffee makers are also available.

Fisher & Paykel launched the Minimal Style line alongside its State of the Art collection at EuroCucina during Milan design week 2026.

The company was founded in New Zealand in 1934. Find out more about the brand and its Minimal Style luxury appliances on its website.

item.content:encoded:
German studio Sauerbruch Hutton and US practice Studio Gang have been selected to redesign German House to reflect the nation's values and create a "civic landmark" just north of the United Nations complex in Manhattan.

Selected by a jury, the redesign will see the recladding and interior redesign of the 325-foot-tall (99-metre-tall) skyscraper, which was originally designed by American studio SLCE Architects in the 1990s and serves as a base of operations for the Consulate General of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Sauerbruch Hutton and Studio Gang, design architect and architect of record, respectively, conceived a structure with bands of colour on the facade, brightening the current grey exterior.

The studios are combining civic presence and technical efficiency to "display the latest German engineering in sustainable construction before a global audience", according to the team.

"We look forward to working with the Bundesbau Baden-Württemberg and Sauerbruch Hutton to help reimagine German House as a more welcoming and sustainable model for civic architecture in New York and within the international diplomatic community," said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

"This project, which holds cultural exchange at its heart, is an exciting opportunity to bring together German design expertise with the proven project delivery in New York City."

The team plans to integrate photovoltaic panels onto the facade while formulating a box-window system that allows for solar shading and the opening of windows to allow for natural ventilation.

These interventions will be made while maintaining the heightened security necessary for a high-profile diplomatic building.

The team also plans to revamp the interior spaces, integrating a "sky lobby with a vertical garden" at mid-tower, which will serve as a meeting point for the Consulate General and the UN mission.

Read:

Eero Saarinen's Black Rock skyscraper refurbished in New York

A restaurant on the upper floors will open onto a shaded garden space.

The choice of renovating, as opposed to building new, was also highlighted by the studios, which noted the carbon benefits of preserving the structure.

"Through careful transformation rather than replacement, the tower is adapted to encourage exchange across departments while extending the life of the building for decades to come," said Sauerbruch Hutton partner Lina Lahiri.

The building will be the first project by Sauerbruch Hutton in the United States.

Other recent Manhattan skyscraper renovations include SOM's renovation of the iconic Lever House and Vocon Architects and MdeAS Architects' renovation of Eero Saarinen's Black Rock skyscraper.

item.content:encoded:
New York architecture studio Diller Scofidio + Renfro has spliced an 1894 brick warehouse building with several glazed volumes to create a home for MIT's School of Architecture and Planning.

The Metropolitan Storage Warehouse building (MET) is located on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts and will house several architecture and design schools, including the Department of Architecture and the Department of Urban Studies and Planning.

The schools will relocate to the converted warehouse from their current location in the neoclassical Building 7, which sits cady corner to the new building.

Originally built in 1894 by local architect Frederic Pope and expanded throughout the decades, the brick warehouse once stored items such as pianos, carriages and furs for Boston's wealthiest families.

The studio's renovation included expanding the building's low ceiling heights and inserting "a series of carved-out voids" along the building's length, while maintaining portions of the original brick facade.

The project included careful "cutting strategies" and the application of new support systems to shift existing loads within the building to make room for modern academic spaces such as studios and makerspaces.

"By creating the necessary high-ceiling studio spaces through the removal of portions of the heavy, archaic masonry floor system, the structural load imposed on the existing columns and wood piles was significantly reduced," said Diller Scofidio + Renfro (DS+R).

"This reduction revealed sufficient reserve capacity within the existing structure to support the newly introduced, lightweight modern floor slabs, which are 'hung' by steel straps from beams supported by the existing columns and wood piles."

This architectural surgery allowed for a light, open, majority column-free interior and was informed by the interventions of Gordon Matta-Clark, according to the studio.

On the interior, the studio left some of the cuttings exposed to showcase the historical cross-sections to students. This can be seen in the sections of the original brick archways that run underneath the floor slabs.

Read:

MIT researchers design Heirloom House concrete components to last "1,000 years"

The programming and studios are now organised around large, double-height spaces, which are traversed via a continuous linear public stair.

They are organised into "neighbourhoods" across the five interconnected volumes of the building. Along one facade of the building, the glass insertions are exposed, while the other side is completely brick.

The studio also maintained details such as the building's fortress-like corner towers and crenellated corbeled cornices, while punching new windows into its two-foot-thick walls.

The team is targeting LEED Gold for the project.

"The techniques used in this adaptive reuse project have a pedagogical objective  –  to expose layers of history and allow students to experience firsthand the possibilities of breathing new life into a relic previously thought to be uninhabitable," said the studio.

DS+R recently adapted a London hangar into a publicly accessible storage facility for the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and is also working on a mass timber building at Boston University.

item.content:encoded:
Indian studio AKSH Architects has completed The Earthen Retreat, a cluster of guesthouses in Pune created by repurposing several small abandoned buildings and coating them with mud and lime plaster.

The 557-square-metre plot was previously occupied by four site offices and storage units that had outlived their original purpose.

While maintaining the existing timber and steel structures of these units, AKSH Architects used natural materials to demonstrate how "forgotten infrastructure" can be transformed into "architecture with lasting cultural, environmental and experiential value".

"The design intervention was intentionally radical," the studio's founder Akash Shingvi told Dezeen.

"Every space was reshaped through sculptural forms, natural mud and lime-plastered surfaces, local materials and fluid spatial planning, making it almost impossible to recognise the original buildings," added Shingvi.

"Our intention was to create an experience that feels timeless, earthy and deeply connected to nature, where architecture is perceived through texture, light and emotion rather than ornamentation."

The four blocks, each of which is divided into two neighbouring guesthouses, are arranged symmetrically around a communal paved patio with a swimming pool at its centre.

Inside, each of The Earthen Retreat's guesthouses contains a bedroom and a bathroom that has been left partially open to the elements, sheltered by a bamboo canopy that allows light and air to filter through.

Read:

Eleena Jamil shades Malaysian guesthouse with bamboo and steel canopy

Textured, lime-plastered walls and ceilings envelop the rooms, finished in earthy shades of beige and dark green, and punctured by arched and curved openings.

Curved forms were also used for built-in benches that extend around half of the bedrooms to form bedside tables, as well as for the bathroom's large, oval-shaped bath and a curved opening into the shower.

Externally, each of the four units has been given a matching rough plaster finish, with their perimeters shaded by the deep overhang of the bamboo roofs above.

"Curved, organic forms replace rigid partitions, allowing movement through the cottage to feel fluid, intuitive and experiential," said Shingvi.

"Since the retreat sits in a tropical setting, it didn't feel right to introduce materials that looked overly refined or disconnected from the place," he added.

"We consciously worked with natural materials that were commonly available in the local context, such as bamboo, lime and mud plaster and timber," he added.

Other projects in India that have recently incorporated mud and earth into their material palette include Aurva Illam near Hyderabad, a home by studio Iki Builds designed to reflect the rocky character of the nearby Deccan Plateau, and the mud-walled Winterfell house, which is woven around existing trees in Tamil Nadu.

The photography is by Harsh Lunavat.

item.content:encoded:
British carmaker Jaguar has revealed a glimpse of its upcoming Type 01 electric car, which has a central divider and "on-demand" screens.

The recently released renders show the interior of Jaguar's Type 01 electric car, which will be the production version of the much-discussed Type 00 concept car that was first revealed in 2024.

Jaguar plans to unveil the car this October.

The renders show a sleek, modern interior divided by a central bar that runs the full length of the car. This makes the Type 01 a four-seat car with distinct seating areas for each of the passengers.

Another notable aspect of the interior is the lack of a giant, central screen – commonly seen in modern electric cars.

A small screen is mounted on the central division, while other "digital interfaces are intelligently applied for control on demand".

"Our holistic design philosophy translates the vehicle's exterior presence into a distinctive interior architecture," said Jaguar's chief interior designer Thomas Holden.

"In contrast to the horizontal interior design norm, we emphasise its dramatic longitudinal nature through the central spine – an architectural statement that creates four individual spaces," he continued.

"With authentic materials, technology on demand and reductive flowing surfaces, Type 01 presents unmistakable drama and theatre that will define the modern luxury automotive interior of the future."

A prototype of the Type 01 will be on display at this week's Monterey Car Week.

The car will be the first released by Jaguar as part of its "complete reset" as it moves to electric-only cars. The reset began with a controversial rebrand at the end of 2024.

Read:

Jaguar's controversial Type 00 concept car spotted driving on the streets of Paris

"Jaguar Type 01 is the first production car to follow our new creative philosophy," said Jaguar managing director Rawdon Glover.

"Unmistakable from every angle, the interior is no different. With Type 01, we wanted every journey to be an occasion, from how it drives to how it looks and how it makes you feel.

"With a confidence-inspiring GT driving position, clean and sophisticated technology and dramatic styling, Type 01 has an interior like no other."

The reset was led by Jaguar Land Rover chief creative officer Gerry McGovern, who departed the company at the end of 2025, a year after the unveiling of the radical Type 00 concept car.
